hints.title: 1 · Name the two operations you need
hints.body: Every call needs a constant-time lookup by key and a constant-time move-to-most-recent. A plain Array gives you order but linear lookup; a plain Hash gives you lookup but no reordering. Write down which structure in Ruby offers both before writing code.

hints.title: 2 · Ruby hashes remember insertion order
hints.body: A Hash iterates keys in insertion order, and deleting then reinserting a key moves it to the end. That is the whole reordering primitive: `h.delete(k); h[k] = v`. The first key in the hash is then always the least recently used one, and `h.shift` removes it.\n\nExample with a different problem: a most-recent-files list keeps `files.delete(path); files[path] = true` on every open, and `files.shift` when it grows past ten.

hints.title: 3 · Check eviction after insertion, and only on insertion
hints.body: Insert or replace first, then evict while size exceeds capacity. Replacing an existing key cannot grow the cache, so it never evicts. A `get` on a missing key must not insert anything and must not change order. Walk the visible test for a replaced key by hand: which key is first in `keys` afterwards?

criteria.title: Eviction and recency are exact
criteria.target: The least recently used key is evicted only when a new key exceeds capacity; `get` and `put` both refresh recency; replacing a key never evicts.
criteria.probe: Which operations change the recency order, and which do not? Give one sequence where a `get` changes which key gets evicted next.
criteria.practice: Write the recency order after each of eight operations by hand before running the suite.

criteria.title: Constant-time operations
criteria.target: `get` and `put` do not scan the entries; the 100,000-operation groups run in bounded time.
criteria.probe: What is the cost of `delete` plus reinsert on a Ruby Hash, and why is `keys` allowed to be linear?
criteria.practice: Replace one constant-time step with a linear scan and observe which hidden group fails.

criteria.title: Capacity one, nil values and odd keys
criteria.target: Capacity one works; a stored `nil` stays an entry that occupies capacity and appears in `keys`, and `get` returning `nil` for it exactly as for an absent key is the contract, not a gap; arrays, strings and integers all work as keys. Whether `get` refreshes recency is rated under correctness, not here.
criteria.probe: `get` returns `nil` both for a stored `nil` and for an absent key, so why must your implementation still tell the two apart internally, and how does your code do that without a sentinel?
criteria.practice: Add a visible test that a stored `nil` still occupies its slot and is returned as `nil` after later puts, and make it pass without special-casing.

criteria.title: Reasoned about the oracle
criteria.target: Predicted a failing sequence before running tests and explained what each failing group means.
criteria.probe: What sequence would expose an off-by-one in the eviction check?
criteria.practice: Before each run, write the expected `keys` for one sequence and compare.

follow_up: Entries now also expire after a fixed time-to-live. Describe what `get` must check, how expiry interacts with the recency order, and what you would measure. Treat this as a separate extension of the original contract.
